{{smaller block|<poem>Fierce in dread silence, on the blasted heath,
Fell ''upas'' sits, the hydra-tree of death.</poem>
{{right|''Erasmus Darwin.''}}}}
'''3.''' Figuratively, something baneful or pernicious from a moral point of view: as, the ''upas'' of drunkenness.

'''upas-tree''' (ū′pas-trē), ''n.'' See ''upas'', 2.

'''upaventure†''', ''adv.'' [< ''up'', ''prep.'', + ''aventure.'' Cf. ''peradventure.''] In case that; if.
{{smaller block|They bade me that I should be busy in all my wits to go as near the sentence and the words as I could, both that were spoken to me and that I spake, ''upaventure'' this writing came another time before the archbishop and his council. {{right|''Bp. Bale'', Select Works, p. 66. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''upbear''' (up-bãr′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To bear, carry, or raise aloft; lift; elevate; sustain aloft.
{{smaller block|<poem>One short sigh of human breath, ''upborne''
Ev’n to the seat of God. ''Milton'', P. L., xi. 147.</poem>
<poem>Swift as on wings of winds ''upborn'' they fly.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Odyssey, viii. 127.}}}}
'''2.''' To support; sustain.
{{smaller block|<poem>His resolve
''Upbore'' him, and firm faith.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}
Language . . . ''upborne'' by . . . thought.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 325.}}}}
'''3†.''' To hold up; commend.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ne him for his desire no shame,
Al were it wist, but in pris and ''upborn''
Of alle lovers, wel more than beforn.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 375.}}}}

'''upbind''' (up-bīnd′), ''v. t.'' To bind up.
{{smaller block|Thy injur’d robes ''up-bind!'' ''Collins'', Ode to Peace, st. 3.}}
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''3.''' Specifically, to reprove with severity; chide.
{{smaller block|Then he began to ''upbraid'' the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done.
{{right|Mat. xi. 20.}}}}

'''4.''' To bring reproach on; be a reproach to.
{{smaller block|How much doth thy kindness ''upbraid'' my wickedness!
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}
Will not the sobriety of the very Turks ''upbraid'' our excesses and debaucheries?
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. iii.}}}}

'''5†.''' To make a subject of reproach or chiding.
{{smaller block|<poem>I would not boast my actions, yet ’tis lawful
To ''upbraid'' my benefits to unthankful men.</poem>
{{right|''Massinger'', Unnatural Combat, i. 1.}}
He who hath done a good turn should so forget it as not to speak of it; but he that boasts it, or ''upbraids'' it, hath paid himself.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living, iv. 8.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' ''Mock'', ''Flout'', etc. See ''taunt''<sup>1</sup>.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To utter upbraidings or reproaches.
{{smaller block|<poem>Have we not known thee slave! of all our host
The man who acts the least ''upbraids'' the most.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, ii. 312.}}
<poem>In vain the envious tongue ''upbraids'';
His name a nation’s heart shall keep
Till morning’s latest sunlight fades
On the blue tablet of the deep!</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Birthday of D. Webster.}}}}

'''upbraid†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''upbræid'', ''upbraide'', ''upbreid'', ''oupbreid''; from the verb.] The act of upbraiding; reproach; contumely; abuse. ''Chapman'', Iliad, vi. 389.

'''upbraider''' (up-brā′dėr), ''n.'' [< ''upbraid'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who upbraids or reproves.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''upbraiding''' (up-brā′ding), ''n.'' '''1.''' The act or language of one who upbraids; severe reproof or reproach.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have too long borne
Your blunt ''upbraidings.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 3. 104.}}}}
'''2.''' Nausea; vomiting. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|''Remors de l’estomac'', The ''vpbraiding'' of the stomacke.
{{right|''Cotgrave.''}}}}

'''upbraiding''' (up-brā′ding), ''p. a.'' Reproachful; chiding.
{{smaller block|<poem>The pouting lip
And sad, ''upbraiding'' eye of the poor girl . . .
Must now be disregarded.</poem>
{{right|''Halleck'', Fanny.}}}}

'''upbraidingly''' (up-brā′ding-li), ''adv.'' In an upbraiding manner. ''B. Jonson'', Discoveries.

'''upbray†''' (up-brā′), ''v.'' A false form of ''upbraid.'' ''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. i. 42.

'''upbray†''' (up-brā′), ''n.'' A false form of ''upbraid.'' ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vi. 50.

'''upbreak''' (up-brāk′), ''v. i.'' To break or force a way upward; come to the surface; appear. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|When from the gloom of the dark earth ''upbreaks'' the tender bloom.
{{right|''Littell’s Living Age'', CLXXV. 66.}}}}

'''upbreak''' (up′brāk), ''n.'' A breaking or bursting up; an upburst. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''upbreaking''' (up-brā′king), ''a.'' Breaking up; dissolving.
{{smaller block|An ''upbreaking'' and disparting storm.
{{right|''J. Wilson'', Lights and Shadows of Scottish Life, p. 104.}}}}

'''upbreathe†''' (up-brēᴛ̵ʜ′), ''v. t.'' To breathe up or out; exhale. ''Marston.''
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''upbreed†''' (up-brēd′), ''v. t.'' To breed up; nurse; train up. ''Holinshed'', Hist. of Scotland.

'''upbring†''', ''v. t.'' To bring up; nourish; educate. ''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. iv. 38.

'''upbringing''' (up′bring-ing), ''n.'' The process of bringing up, nourishing, or maintaining; training; education. ''Carlyle'', Sartor Resartus (1831), p. 68.

'''upbuild''' (up-bild′), ''v. t.'' To build up; edify; establish. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Plainly the science of zoölogy could not have been ''upbuilt'' without it. {{right|''Proc. Soc. Psych. Research'', I. 149.}}}}

'''upbuilding''' (up-bil′ding), ''n.'' The act or process of building up, in any sense; edification; establishment.

'''upbuoyance''' (up-boi′ans), ''n.'' The act of buoying up or uplifting. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Me rather, bright guests, with your wings of ''upbuoyance''
Bear aloft to your homes, to your banquets of joyance.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', Visit of the Gods.}}}}

'''upburst''' (up′bėrst), ''n.'' A bursting up; a breaking a way up and through; an uprush: as, an ''upburst'' of lava. ''H. O. Forbes'', Eastern Archipelago, p. 232.

'''upby''' (up′bī), ''adv.'' [< ''up'' + ''by''<sup>1</sup>.] A little way further on; up the way. [Scotch.]

'''upcast''' (up-kȧst′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''upcasten''; < ''up'' + ''cast''.] To cast or throw up.
{{smaller block|Custance and eek hir child the see ''upcaste''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 808.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''upcast''' (up′kȧst), ''a.'' '''1.''' Cast up: a term used in bowling.—'''2.''' Thrown or turned upward; directed up: as, ''upcast'' eyes. ''Addison,'' To Sir Godfrey Kneller, l. 61.

'''upcast''' (up′kȧst), ''n.'' [< ''upcast, v.''] '''1.''' The act of casting or hurling upward, or the state of being cast upward; also, that which is cast upward; an upthrow.
{{smaller block|Thus fall to the ground the views of those who have sought for the cause of these movements in the different specific gravities of the air in cyclones and anticyclones, in the ''upcast'' to which the air must be subject in a cyclone.
{{right|''Nature,'' XLIII. 16.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''bowling,'' a cast; a throw.
{{smaller block|Was there ever man had such luck! When I kiss’d the jack upon an ''up-cast'' to be hit away!
{{right|''Shak.,'' Cymbeline, ii. 1. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''mining,'' the shaft or passage of any kind through which the air is taken out of a mine; the out-take: the opposite of ''downcast'' (which see) and ''downtake.'' {{smaller|''Intake'' and ''out-take'' are terms more generally applied to drifts, levels, or horizontal passages; ''downcast'' and ''upcast'' to vertical or inclined shafts.}} '''4.''' An upward current of air passing through a shaft or the like.—'''5.''' The state of being overturned; an upset. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|What wi’ the ''upcast'' and terror that I got a wee while syne, . . . my head is sair eneugh.
{{right|''Scott.''}}}}
'''6.''' A taunt; a reproach. [Scotch.]

'''upcaught''' (up-kât′), ''a.'' Caught or seized up.
{{smaller block|She bears ''upcaught'' a mariner away.
{{right|''Cowper,'' Odyssey, xii. 118.}}}}

'''upchance†''', ''adv.'' [< ME. ''upchaunce''; < ''up, prep.,'' + ''chance.'' Cf. ''perchance.''] Perchance; perhaps.
readings.c2s4:
{{smaller block|''Up-chaunce ye may them mete.''
{{right|''Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 81).}}}}

'''upcheer†''' (up-chēr′), ''v. t.'' To cheer up; enliven. ''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. i. 44.

'''Upchurch pottery.''' See ''pottery''.

'''upclimb''' (up-klīm′), ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' To climb up; ascend. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Up-clomb'' the shadowy pine above the woven copse.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lotos-Eaters.}}}}

'''upcoil''' (up-koil′), ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' To wind up into a coil; coil.

'''upcoming''' (up′kum-ing), ''n.'' The act or process of coming up; uprising. ''Athenæum'', No. 3218, p. 831.

'''up-country''' (up′kun″tri), ''adv.'' Toward the interior; away from the seaboard. [Colloq.]

'''up-country''' (up′kun′tri), ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' The interior of the country. [Colloq.]

'''II.''' ''a.'' Being or living away from the seaboard; interior: as, an ''up-country'' village. [Colloq.]

'''upcurl''' (up-kėrl′), ''v. t.'' To curl or wreathe upward. ''Southey'', Thalaba, iv., 36.

'''up-curved''' (up′kėrvd), ''a.'' Curved upward; recurved: as, in entomology, an ''up-curved'' margin.

'''updelve†''' (up-delv′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''updelven''; < ''up'' + ''delve''.] To dig up. ''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 174.

'''updive''' (up-dīv′), ''v. i.'' To rise to the surface. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Thence make thy fame ''updive''.
{{right|''Davies'', Microcosmos, p. 81.}}}}

'''updraw''' (up-drâ′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''updrawen''; < ''up'' + ''draw''.] '''1.''' To draw up. ''Cowper'', Iliad, i.—'''2.''' Figuratively, to train or bring up.

'''upflow''' (up-flō′), ''v. i.'' To ascend; stream up. ''Southey'', Thalaba, ii. [Rare.]

'''upflow''' (up′flō), ''n.'' A flowing up; rise: as, an ''upflow'' of air. ''Philos. Mag.'', 5th ser., XXX. 501.

'''upfling''' (up-fling′), ''v. t.'' To fling or throw up. [Rare.]

'''upfolded''' (up-fōl′ded), ''a.'' Folded up. ''J. Wilson'', Lights and Shadows of Scottish Life. [Rare.]

'''upgather''' (up-gaᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v. t.'' To gather up or together; contract. ''Spenser''. [Rare.]

'''upgaze''' (up-gāz′), ''v. i.'' To gaze upward; look steadily upward. ''Byron'', Childe Harold, ii. [Rare.]

'''upgirt''' (up-gėrt′), ''a.'' Girded up. ''The Atlantic'', LXVI. 35. [Rare.]

'''upgive†''' (up-giv′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''upgiven''; < ''up'' + ''give''<sup>1</sup>.] To give up or out; yield. ''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1569.

'''upgoing''' (up′gō-ing), ''a.'' Going up; moving upward. ''Lancet'', No. 3479, p. 955.

'''upgrow''' (up-grō′), ''v. i.'' To grow up. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 677. [Rare.]

'''upgrowth''' (up′grōth), ''n.'' '''1.''' The process of growing up; development; rise and progress; upspringing. ''J. R. Green''.

{{right|''The Century'', XXXV. 2.}}}}

'''2.''' That which grows up or out: as, cartilaginous ''upgrowths''. ''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., i. 22.

'''upgush''' (up-gush′), ''v. i.'' To gush upward. [Rare.]

'''upgush''' (up′gush), ''n.'' A gushing upward: as, an ''upgush'' of feeling. ''G. S. Hall'', German Culture, p. 155. [Rare.]

'''uphand''' (up′hand), ''a.'' Lifted by the hand or hands: as, an ''uphand'' sledge (a large hammer lifted with both hands).

{{right|''Moxon'', Mechanical Exercises.}}}}

'''uphang''' (up-hang′), ''v. t.'' To hang up; suspend or affix aloft. ''Spenser'', Visions of Bellay, vi. [Rare.]

{{right|''Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 81).}}}}

'''upcheer†''' (up-chēr′), ''v. t.'' To cheer up; enliven. ''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. i. 44.

'''Upchurch pottery.''' See ''pottery''.

'''upclimb''' (up-klīm′), ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' To climb up; ascend. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Up-clomb'' the shadowy pine above the woven copse.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lotos-Eaters.}}}}

'''upcoil''' (up-koil′), ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' To wind up into a coil; coil.

'''upcoming''' (up′kum-ing), ''n.'' The act or process of coming up; uprising. ''Athenæum'', No. 3218, p. 831.

'''up-country''' (up′kun″tri), ''adv.'' Toward the interior; away from the seaboard. [Colloq.]

'''up-country''' (up′kun′tri), ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' The interior of the country. [Colloq.]

'''II.''' ''a.'' Being or living away from the seaboard; interior: as, an ''up-country'' village. [Colloq.]

'''upcurl''' (up-kėrl′), ''v. t.'' To curl or wreathe upward. ''Southey'', Thalaba, iv., 36.

'''up-curved''' (up′kėrvd), ''a.'' Curved upward; recurved: as, in entomology, an ''up-curved'' margin.

'''updelve†''' (up-delv′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''updelven''; < ''up'' + ''delve''.] To dig up. ''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 174.

'''updive''' (up-dīv′), ''v. i.'' To rise to the surface. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Thence make thy fame ''updive''.
{{right|''Davies'', Microcosmos, p. 81.}}}}

'''updraw''' (up-drâ′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''updrawen''; < ''up'' + ''draw''.] '''1.''' To draw up. ''Cowper'', Iliad, i.—'''2.''' Figuratively, to train or bring up.
<poem>A knight, whom from childhode
He had ''updrawe'' into manhode.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., v. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''updress†''' (up-dres′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''updressen''; < ''up'' + ''dress.''] To set up; prepare.
{{smaller block|<poem>He wolde ''updresse''
Engyns, bothe more and lesse,
To cast at us, by every side.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 7067.}}}}

'''upend''' (up-end′), ''v. t.'' To set on end, as a barrel.
{{smaller block|An approaching heavy sea may carry the boat away on its front, and turn it broadside on, or ''up-end'' it.
{{right|''Luce'', Seamanship, p. 611.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Upending-tongs''', heavy tongs with a swinging support, used in iron-works to turn the bloom, that the hammer may strike upon its end.}}

'''upfill''' (up-fil′), ''v. t.'' To fill up; make full. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|A cup . . . to the brim ''upfild.'' {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. iii. 42.}}}}

'''upflow''' (up-flō′), ''v. i.'' To ascend; stream up. ''Southey'', Thalaba, ii. [Rare.]

'''upflow''' (up′flō), ''n.'' A flowing up; rise: as, an ''upflow'' of air. ''Philos. Mag.'', 5th ser., XXX. 501.

'''upfling''' (up-fling′), ''v. t.'' To fling or throw up. [Rare.]

'''upfolded''' (up-fōl′ded), ''a.'' Folded up. ''J. Wilson'', Lights and Shadows of Scottish Life. [Rare.]

'''upgather''' (up-gaᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v. t.'' To gather up or together; contract. ''Spenser''. [Rare.]

'''upgaze''' (up-gāz′), ''v. i.'' To gaze upward; look steadily upward. ''Byron'', Childe Harold, ii. [Rare.]

'''upgirt''' (up-gėrt′), ''a.'' Girded up. ''The Atlantic'', LXVI. 35. [Rare.]

'''upgive†''' (up-giv′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''upgiven''; < ''up'' + ''give''<sup>1</sup>.] To give up or out; yield. ''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1569.

'''upgoing''' (up′gō-ing), ''a.'' Going up; moving upward. ''Lancet'', No. 3479, p. 955.

'''upgrow''' (up-grō′), ''v. i.'' To grow up. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 677. [Rare.]

'''upgrowth''' (up′grōth), ''n.'' '''1.''' The process of growing up; development; rise and progress; upspringing. ''J. R. Green''.
{{smaller block|The prelate still keeping some shreds of civil power notwithstanding the ''upgrowth'' of the plebeian layman’s power.
{{right|''The Century'', XXXV. 2.}}}} '''2.''' That which grows up or out: as, cartilaginous ''upgrowths''. ''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., i. 22.

'''upgush''' (up-gush′), ''v. i.'' To gush upward. [Rare.]

'''upgush''' (up′gush), ''n.'' A gushing upward: as, an ''upgush'' of feeling. ''G. S. Hall'', German Culture, p. 155. [Rare.]

'''uphand''' (up′hand), ''a.'' Lifted by the hand or hands: as, an ''uphand'' sledge (a large hammer lifted with both hands).
{{smaller block|The ''uphand'' sledge is used by underworkmen.
{{right|''Moxon'', Mechanical Exercises.}}}}

'''uphang''' (up-hang′), ''v. t.'' To hang up; suspend or affix aloft. ''Spenser'', Visions of Bellay, vi. [Rare.]
